explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The letter says, "…just as you have received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to walk in Him…" (Colossians 2:6). Walking is one step after another, day after day. It's like stamping a batch of cookies, one at a time, until the tray is full.

Close, but the letter doesn't say waiting. It says to "…continue to walk in Him…" (Colossians 2:6). I did plenty of waiting in the back of a junk drawer, and walking is a lot more fun. Walking means moving, and you keep moving with Christ as Lord.

The letter says they already received Christ Jesus as Lord, so there's nothing to go hunting for. What comes next is to "…continue to walk in Him…" (Colossians 2:6). Searching for Him now would be like tearing up the house for your glasses while they're sitting on your head. You've got Him, so walk with Him.

Yes, that's what the letter says: "…established in the faith as you were taught…" (Colossians 2:7). They're to stay planted in the faith they were taught. No need to go hunting for a brand new recipe.

This one's true. The letter tells them to be "…established in the faith as you were taught…" (Colossians 2:7). The faith they were taught is what they're to be established in. So no, it isn't false, but it's a sneaky one when you read it fast.

That's right. The letter says this philosophy and empty deception is based on human tradition and the spiritual forces of the world "…rather than on Christ." (Colossians 2:8). So the contrast here is with Christ. Empty deception, like a pretty box with no cookies inside.

Moses, Israel's leader, is a good name to know, but he isn't in this verse. The letter says the philosophy is based on human tradition and the spiritual forces of the world "…rather than on Christ." (Colossians 2:8). The contrast is with Christ, not with a person from the past.

Angels don't show up in this verse at all. The letter says the deception is based on human tradition and the spiritual forces of the world "…rather than on Christ." (Colossians 2:8). Everything here gets measured against Christ, so that's the word that fits the blank.

Yes, bodily, and that's the word the letter uses. "For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form." (Colossians 2:9). All the fullness, not a sample or a taste. That's why nothing clever needs to be added on top of Him.
Not borrowed, friend. The letter says "…all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form." (Colossians 2:9). Nothing about it is on loan or short on anything. It's all of it, and it's in Christ.

I can see why hidden sounds mysterious, but that's not the word. The letter says "…all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form." (Colossians 2:9). The word is bodily, and the verse says that fullness dwells in Christ. All of it, in Christ.

This one says they still need something more, and the letter says the opposite. "And you have been made complete in Christ…" (Colossians 2:10). Complete means nothing is missing. You don't send a finished cookie box back to be filled.
Right, it's false. The letter says, "…you have been made complete in Christ…" (Colossians 2:10). Nothing is left over that you need to go find somewhere else. In Him, the job is done.
That's it. The letter says Christ "…is the head over every ruler and authority." (Colossians 2:10). Every one, with nobody left out. That's a big title, and it's why we can stand firm.

The letter doesn't shrink it down that small. It says Christ "…is the head over every ruler and authority." (Colossians 2:10). The apostles aren't even mentioned in this verse. His headship covers every ruler and authority.

Nice try, but the circle is much bigger. Christ "…is the head over every ruler and authority." (Colossians 2:10). The believers in Colossae are the ones who were made complete in Him, but the headship goes far past one town. I'd say that's good news for everybody.

Yes, their sinful nature. The letter says, "In Him you were also circumcised, in the putting off of your sinful nature…" (Colossians 2:11). Something heavy gets taken off. I know that feeling, like finally taking off an apron after a very long bake.

The letter says nothing about money here. What gets put off is "…your sinful nature…" (Colossians 2:11). Wealth is never mentioned in this verse. So keep your wallet, friend, because the thing coming off is the sinful nature.

Your family name stays right where it is. The letter says the circumcision was "…in the putting off of your sinful nature…" (Colossians 2:11). Nothing is said here about names or families. What comes off is the sinful nature.
That's right. It was "…the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands." (Colossians 2:11). The contrast is between Christ and human hands. Christ is the one who performed it.

Priests aren't in this verse. It says "…the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands." (Colossians 2:11). The contrast is between what Christ does and what human hands do. So no priest is needed for this one.

Laws aren't named here. The letter says the circumcision was "…performed by Christ and not by human hands." (Colossians 2:11). Hands are the picture of human effort. This was Christ's work, from start to finish.

Yes! "And having been buried with Him in baptism, you were raised with Him…" (Colossians 2:12). Buried is not the end of that sentence. The letter says they were raised through their faith in the power of God, who raised Him from the dead. They were raised with Him, and that's the part that gets me excited.

explanations.answer: They waited for Him to return
explanations.explanation: The letter doesn't say that here. After being buried with Him in baptism, it says "…you were raised with Him…" (Colossians 2:12). The sentence goes straight from buried to raised. My ovens stay ready for His return, but that's a different verse.

explanations.answer: They were sent out to find Him
explanations.explanation: They didn't have to go find Him, because they were already with Him. The letter says they were buried with Him and then "…you were raised with Him…" (Colossians 2:12). Raised with Him means they were right there with Him. No search party needed.

That's the answer. They were raised "…through your faith in the power of God, who raised Him from the dead." (Colossians 2:12). The power belongs to God, and faith is how they trust it. It's the same power that raised Christ.

That's not how the letter puts it. They were raised "…through your faith in the power of God, who raised Him from the dead." (Colossians 2:12). Law-keeping isn't mentioned in the verse. Faith in God's power is the way.

Good works are a fine thing, but they aren't what raised anybody here. The letter says "…through your faith in the power of God, who raised Him from the dead." (Colossians 2:12). The power is God's, so it isn't about anyone lifting themselves up. They were raised through faith in what He can do.

Yes. "When you were dead in your trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your sinful nature, God made you alive with Christ." (Colossians 2:13). Dead to alive. Notice who does the work: God. That's about as big a turnaround as there is.

explanations.answer: Gave them rules to fix it
explanations.explanation: The letter doesn't say God handed them a list. It says, "…God made you alive with Christ." (Colossians 2:13). Rules can't fix being dead, and the verse never says they do. God acted, and He made them alive with Christ.

explanations.answer: Waited for them to wake up
explanations.explanation: The letter doesn't describe God waiting. It says they were "…dead in your trespasses…" and then "…God made you alive with Christ." (Colossians 2:13). God is the one who acted.
That's the word. "He forgave us all our trespasses…" (Colossians 2:13). All, with nothing held back or kept on a shelf for later. That's a lot of grace.

Most sounds nice, but it isn't what the letter says. "He forgave us all our trespasses…" (Colossians 2:13). Most would leave some behind, and the verse says all. Not a single crumb left on the counter.
Some would be a smaller gift than the one given. The letter says, "He forgave us all our trespasses…" (Colossians 2:13). That's all of them, not a handful. I'd say that's worth a happy dance.
That's right. The letter says He was "…having canceled the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us." (Colossians 2:14). Canceled means it's no longer owed. The bill is gone.

This one's true, friend. The letter says God forgave us all our trespasses, "…having canceled the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us." (Colossians 2:14). So the debt was canceled, and that's why True is the answer. I know, a bill getting canceled seems too good to be true, and yet here it is.
Yes, the cross. The letter says, "He took it away, nailing it to the cross!" (Colossians 2:14). That debt isn't just set aside, it's taken away. The cross is where the verse says it went.
An altar isn't in the verse. The letter says, "He took it away, nailing it to the cross!" (Colossians 2:14). The cross is where the debt went. The altar is a good answer for a different passage.
No gate here, friend. The letter says, "He took it away, nailing it to the cross!" (Colossians 2:14). That's the spot where the debt was dealt with.

That's it. The letter says, "…having disarmed the powers and authorities…" (Colossians 2:15). God is the one who did the disarming. Picture the scary guy showing up with nothing but an empty oven mitt.
Bargained with isn't the word the letter uses. It says, "…having disarmed the powers and authorities…" (Colossians 2:15). God is the one who did the disarming.
Ignored isn't the word the letter uses. It says, "…having disarmed the powers and authorities…" (Colossians 2:15). God is the one who did the disarming, and disarmed is what the verse says.

Not quite, friend. The letter says God "…made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross." (Colossians 2:15). Nothing in that verse says it happened somewhere nobody could see. It says He made a public spectacle of them. So True doesn't fit what the verse says.

Right, it's false. The letter says God "…made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross." (Colossians 2:15). The verse says a public spectacle, not somewhere nobody could see. The triumph came by the cross.
